title: Meet the Community
text: The Global RIver-lanD (GRID) Database began as a collaboration among researchers at Syracuse University, Texas A&M University, and Yale University. Tao Wen and Shuang Zhang continue on the GRID management team. The proposed GRID-SI project brings together a broader team to develop reusable hydrogeochemical datasets and software workflows.

title: Methods and Interpretation
text: GRID research products combine river observations, watershed information, and analytical workflows. Methods and quality controls depend on the release. The examples below describe documented approaches in public products; consult each linked record and article for its full methods and limitations.

title: Methods and Interpretation
text:
Observations, derived estimates, and predictions

Observations are measurements reported by a source monitoring program, with its sampling methods, units, and quality information.
Derived estimates are calculated from observations, for example through temporal aggregation, discharge weighting, or geochemical inverse modeling.
Model predictions estimate values using fitted relationships and environmental inputs. Their interpretation depends on the training data, validation design, and prediction domain.

Keep these categories distinct when combining products or reporting results. Spatial and temporal aggregation can affect the questions a dataset can answer.

title: Methods and Interpretation
text:
Documented product workflows

U.S. river salinization and alkalinization
The 226-site release combines sodium and alkalinity data with 32 watershed properties. The associated study uses machine learning to predict monthly-aggregated sodium and alkalinity fluxes and examine their relationships with human and natural watershed characteristics. Consult the article and data and code for site selection, processing, and model evaluation.


Northern Gulf of Mexico river–ocean database
ROcD-nGoM brings together river chemistry and discharge with coastal ocean and satellite data. Its river products distinguish observations from daily concentrations and fluxes estimated using the USGS WRTDS model. The repository record describes outlier flags and cleaned monthly, seasonal, and annual aggregates. See the data descriptor for the harmonization approach.


River weathering and machine learning
The weathering data and code release documents an R workflow linking USGS chemistry, InveR geochemical inverse modeling, watershed predictors, and XGBoost. It includes derived analysis tables and code for model training, SHAP interpretation, spatial prediction, and uncertainty analysis. The archived README describes nested cross-validation and bootstrap uncertainty estimation. These are methods documented for this study, rather than a single validation protocol for all GRID products.

title: Methods and Interpretation
text:
Responsible interpretation and reuse
Read the data definitions and methods before selecting fields or combining products. Check units, missing values, source identifiers, aggregation periods, and whether a value is measured or estimated. Model relationships and SHAP summaries describe patterns in fitted models; they do not by themselves establish causation. Uncertainty intervals should be interpreted in light of the sources of uncertainty included in the analysis.
Cite the release used and its associated methods sources. Data-use guidance explains how to find release-specific terms. Contact the project team about provenance, a suspected error, or a proposed new use.

title: Coverage and Scope
section: Choosing data for a research question
text:
Choosing data for a research question
Check the selected release for the variables, locations, sampling period, units, and processing level needed for your analysis. A watershed property may represent a spatial or temporal aggregate, while a river measurement represents a particular sampling location and time. A fine-resolution environmental input does not establish the resolution or accuracy of a derived river product.
Use Data Access for repository links and Methods for product-specific distinctions. Contact the project team about coverage beyond the released products.

title: About GRID
text:
A river sample reflects water moving through a landscape. Interpreting its chemistry requires information about the contributing watershed: its geology, climate, soils, land cover, and human activities. Those observations and contextual data often reside in different sources, with different units, methods, and coverage.
The Global RIver-lanD (GRID) project brings river hydrogeochemical observations and watershed information together to support catchment science. GRID-DB refers to the database; GRID also includes research outputs, analysis code, and teaching resources.

title: About GRID
text:
What is available now

A dated inventory and coverage summary describing the scope of GRID’s assembled holdings.
Released datasets and code for specific river and river–ocean studies, with persistent repository links.
Teaching resources for investigating water quality and working with environmental data.
A research community spanning hydrogeochemistry, watershed science, and computational methods.

Each release has its own geographic coverage, variables, methods, and reuse conditions. The inventory totals are not a claim that every observation is available in a single public download.

title: About GRID
text:
Scientific questions
GRID supports research on how weathering and human activities shape river chemistry. Questions include how different mineral sources and reactions contribute to alkalinity, sulfate, and salinity; how watershed context helps explain their spatial variation; and how source attribution affects interpretations of weathering-related carbon uptake or release.
Published outputs provide examples of these approaches. Methods and interpretation guidance explain why observations, derived quantities, and predictions must be distinguished.

title: About GRID
text:
The next stage
GRID-SI is the proposed development program for better-documented chemistry, reviewed station–catchment links, and reusable computational workflows. Its initial target is a North American reference release, with a bounded test of workflow portability beyond North America. These are development plans, not a claim of an awarded project or completed services.
Explore the roadmap · Get involved

title: Contribute Data
text: We welcome river hydrogeochemical observations and associated watershed information from researchers, government agencies, community organizations, industry, and river commissions.

title: Contribute Data
text:
Start a contribution discussion
Contact the project team with a brief description or a link to an existing public dataset. Include the following information where available:

Scope: variables, locations, observation period, number of sites or records, and file formats.
Provenance: original collectors or providers, sampling and analytical methods, source identifiers, and any previous processing.
Metadata: units, detection limits, quality flags, missing-value codes, coordinates and coordinate reference system, and watershed identifiers.
Rights and credit: data owner, existing license or use restrictions, preferred citation, and contributor contact.
Release timing: whether the data are already public and any requested embargo or other access conditions.

These details help the team assess scientific fit, documentation, and the work needed to integrate the contribution. A published repository record or a small, shareable example is a useful starting point.

title: Contribute Data
text:
Unpublished or restricted data
Contact the team before transferring unpublished, confidential, sensitive, or third-party restricted material so that handling, permissions, and any proposed release timing can be discussed. A comprehensive contribution and embargo policy is under review; this page does not establish an embargo duration or promise access restrictions.
For released products, consult the data-use guidance and the terms in each repository record.

title: Database Overview
text: The Global RIver-lanD (GRID) project brings together river hydrogeochemistry, watershed properties, and derived research products to support Earth-surface science. Linking river observations with environmental context helps researchers investigate weathering, elemental transport, water quality, and human influences on river systems.

title: Database Overview
text:
GRID at a glance
As of October 19, 2026, the project inventory includes 154,577 sites, 91 hydrogeochemical variables, and 139 watershed properties drawn from 19 property sources.
These are project-wide totals. Variable availability, sampling periods, and watershed information differ among sites. The inventory includes more material than the public releases linked on this website; the totals do not imply that every record is publicly downloadable. Explore coverage and scope.

title: Database Overview
section: From observations to reusable research products
text:
From observations to reusable research products
GRID outputs connect compiled observations and watershed information with derived datasets and analysis code. Released examples address river salinization and alkalinization, river–ocean connections, and rock-weathering fluxes. They show how integrated data can support geochemical modeling and AI-enabled discovery.
Browse data and code highlights for each product’s scope, methods, creators, license, and persistent identifier. Read about methods and interpretation to distinguish observations, derived estimates, and model predictions.

title: Database Overview
text:
Access and participation
Published releases are available through their repository records. Start with Data Access to download them. For access to other GRID holdings or collaboration on a specific research question, contact the project team.
We welcome contributions of river observations and associated metadata. Contribute data to discuss scope, provenance, reuse permissions, and release timing with the team.

title: ROcD-nGoM: A River–Ocean Database for the Northern Gulf of Mexico
text:
River monitoring sites around the northern Gulf of Mexico, grouped into western, northern, and eastern locations.
This GRID project output connects river and ocean information for the northern Gulf of Mexico. It includes river chemistry and discharge for 54 rivers, streams, and bayous, together with 17 chemical and physical ocean parameters from the Gulf of Mexico Coastal Ocean Observing System and MODIS and SeaWiFS satellite sensors.
The release distinguishes river observations from daily concentrations and fluxes estimated using the USGS WRTDS model. It provides data with outlier flags and cleaned monthly, seasonal, and annual aggregates. Consult the documentation for the sampling coverage and processing applied to each parameter.

title: River Weathering Data and Machine-Learning Workflows
text:
This GRID project output combines USGS river chemistry and watershed information to examine relationships between land cover and rock-weathering fluxes. The release includes derived data tables, watershed predictor objects, and R code linking geochemical inverse modeling with XGBoost, model interpretation, and uncertainty analysis.
The workflow estimates silicate- and carbonate-derived alkalinity fluxes and generates predictions across the contiguous United States. It provides an example of how compiled river observations and environmental context can support AI-enabled research.

The archive contains geochemical flux estimates, watershed predictor objects, and merged analysis tables. Its README documents 27 study-specific watershed predictors and code for InveR modeling, nested cross-validation, SHAP interpretation, spatial prediction, and bootstrap uncertainty estimation. Follow the archived documentation for required inputs, local path configuration, R packages, and cluster-based steps.
The archived flux table contains 1,153 unique sites; the merged flux-and-predictor table contains 1,084. These are table-specific counts, not necessarily the sample size of each fitted model or the total number of GRID sites. The release’s derived annual and seasonal summaries should be distinguished from individual observations and from predictions generated by the modeling code.

text:

Use the release DOI to identify this archived package. The underlying study workflow is described in the manuscript titled Human modification of land cover reshapes rock weathering fluxes across the contiguous United States.

title: GRID-SI Development Roadmap
text: Status: proposed development, October 19, 2026. GRID-SI builds on GRID-DB and its existing research outputs. The activities below depend on project support; they are not announcements of an NSF award, operational services, or open funding opportunities.

title: GRID-SI Development Roadmap
text:
Scientific purpose
The proposed work asks how weathering pathways and human inputs control river alkalinity, sulfate, and salinity, and when resolving those contributions changes the inferred carbon consequences of weathering. An initial North American reference release would connect river observations to reviewed catchments and their hydrologic and landscape context. Existing global holdings would support a selected test of portability beyond North America.

title: GRID-SI Development Roadmap
text:
Data documentation and quality
Planned work includes harmonizing measurements, recovering missing metadata from source documentation, and retaining original values and analytical qualifications. Documentation would distinguish observed, converted, imputed, and modeled values and record source information and processing decisions.

title: GRID-SI Development Roadmap
text:
Station and catchment links
The project proposes testing vision-language-assisted matching of sampling locations to river reaches against conventional methods. Hydrologic checks and expert review would assess candidate matches, with unresolved alternatives and their uncertainty retained.

title: GRID-SI Development Roadmap
text:
Reusable workflows and scientific evaluation
Proposed Python packages would connect station matching and watershed-property calculation with inverse modeling and machine-learning prediction. Tested notebooks would demonstrate analysis and visualization. Selected LLM skills would call the same code modules with reviewable inputs and saved settings.
Evaluation would compare starting and enhanced records, including source attribution and prediction in catchments withheld from model development. Planned benchmarks would document partitions, baselines, evaluation scripts, and limitations together.

title: GRID-SI Development Roadmap
text:
Contributions and participation
A versioned resource catalog is proposed to connect data and code distributed across established repositories. Catalog discovery and acceptance into a scientifically reviewed GRID release would be separate decisions. Data owners would retain control over private-data transfers and publication.
The proposal includes five two-day hackathons and six pilot awards, with opportunities for early-career researchers to develop datasets, workflow modules, and analysis notebooks. No applications are open through this page. Dates, eligibility, and award terms would be announced if the program proceeds. Public notebooks and Waterlines discussions are also proposed to support teaching and science communication.

title: GRID-SI Development Roadmap
text:
People and progress
The core proposal team and advisory members bring complementary expertise in river chemistry, geoscience data, and software. Future progress updates would link completed outputs and their release documentation. Current releases remain available through Data Access.
To discuss a research need or possible contribution, contact the project.

title: Investigating Potential Methane Sources in Pennsylvania Streams
text:
Investigate three hypothetical water-supply complaints involving methane in Pennsylvania surface waters. Students use Shale Network observations and nearby well records to consider multiple possible methane sources. Detecting methane alone does not establish a leaking oil or gas well.

Audience: Intermediate undergraduate hydrology students.
Estimated time: 2 hours.
Tools: HydroClient, the Pennsylvania DEP Oil and Gas Mapping Tool, and EDWIN well records.
Creators: Liza Brazil, Susan L. Brantley, Jennifer Z. Williams, Seth Pelepko, Stew Beattie, Kyle Homman, and Andrew Nyblade.
Host: Science Education Resource Center at Carleton College (SERC).

The cases cover Chartiers Creek, Black Moshannon Lake, and Sugar Run. Instructions guide students through finding observations, examining nearby wells, and considering alternative explanations.

title: Can River Chemistry Reveal Catchment Lithology?
text:
Developed by Tao Wen for the IAMG 2026 short course, this guided exercise uses river chemistry to distinguish carbonate-dominated catchments from those dominated by crystalline silicate rocks. Learners compare a linear classifier with a small neural network in PyTorch.

Audience: Geoscientists with basic Python skills; no prior PyTorch, deep-learning, or hydrogeochemistry experience required.
Estimated time: 40–45 minutes.
Tools: Google Colab on a free CPU runtime; no GPU or manual data upload required. Local Jupyter instructions are also available.
Developer: Tao Wen, Syracuse University.

title: Can River Chemistry Reveal Catchment Lithology?
text:
Learning goals

Define predictors and target classes from a geoscience question.
Split data before fitting transformations, then train and compare models.
Evaluate class imbalance and interpret classification metrics.
Experiment with activation functions and discuss limits of geographic transfer.

A random station split tests performance in similar sampled settings. It does not establish transfer to unfamiliar regions or prove that lithology alone controls river chemistry.

title: A Machine Learning Approach to Freshwater Analysis
text:
This summary refers to Dan Bernardi’s Syracuse University article, published June 12, 2023.
Researchers from Syracuse University and Texas A&M University used observations from 226 U.S. river-monitoring sites and 32 watershed characteristics to model monthly sodium and alkalinity. The work examined how human activity and environmental conditions relate to river chemistry.
Population density and impervious surfaces were important predictors in the sodium model. Climatic and hydrogeological variables were important in the alkalinity model. These predictive associations help frame further investigation; feature importance alone does not demonstrate a causal pathway or quantify net carbon removal.
